subject: Augustine of Hippo

text_used.text: Augustine's own words are checked against the unrevised NPNF translations, downloaded whole from CCEL as plain text (vols. 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 of the first series, all marked Public Domain). The Confessions are J. G. Pilkington's (1886), which keeps Thee and Thou. Possidius's Life is Herbert T. Weiskotten's translation (Princeton, 1919). 'exact' is the text as printed, with footnote numbers taken out. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God.
text_used.source: CCEL cache files npnf101.txt to npnf108.txt; tertullian.org transcription of Weiskotten
text_used.note: New Advent's copies of the same translations were revised by Kevin Knight (Thee and Thou become You; some words changed). The site's existing quiz lines use New Advent's wording, so section 11 checks them against New Advent and says where CCEL differs. For the saint page, prefer the unrevised CCEL wording. CCEL chapter pages for Confessions Books I and II use the ids vi.I_1 and vi.II_1; Books III to X use lower-case ids (vi.iii.xii). All chapter links below were opened (HTTP 200, right heading).

born.text: Born 13 November 354 at Thagaste (Tagaste) in Numidia, North Africa. Today this is Souk Ahras in Algeria.
born.source: Augustine, On the Happy Life, 6: 'Idibus Novembris mihi natalis dies erat' (quoted in Schaff's Prolegomena, NPNF1-01, note 2); Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), 'Life of St. Augustine of Hippo' (Portalie): 'born at Tagaste on 13 November, 354. Tagaste, now Souk-Ahras'; Britannica, 'Saint Augustine', quick facts: 'November 13, 354, Tagaste, Numidia [now Souk Ahras, Algeria]'
born.note: The day comes from Augustine himself: the Ides of November was his birthday. The year 354 is agreed by the Catholic Encyclopedia, Schaff and Britannica.

grew_up.text: At Thagaste. He went to school at Madauros (Madaura) and then Carthage. His father Patricius was a pagan until near his death. His mother Monica was a Christian.
grew_up.source: Confessions, Book II, chapter 3 (Madaura, Carthage, his father 'a freeman of Thagaste'); Book IX, chapter 9 (Monica won her husband 'in the very end of his earthly life'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1907): 'his father, Patricius ... was still a pagan'
grew_up.note: Possidius (chapter 1) says he was born 'of honorable Christian parents of curial rank'. The Confessions show his father was baptised only near the end. Say 'a pagan father who was baptised before he died' to be safe.

died.text: Died 28 August 430 at Hippo Regius, today Annaba in Algeria. He had a fever. It was the third month of the Vandal siege of his city.
died.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 29: 'in the third month of the siege he succumbed to fever and began to suffer in his last illness'; Schaff, Prolegomena, note 2: the date 28 August 430 from the Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine; Catholic Encyclopedia (1907): 'departed ... on 28 August, 430, in the seventy-sixth year of his age'; Merriam-Webster, 'Hippo': 'ancient city in northern Africa south of modern Annaba, Algeria'
died.note: Possidius does not give the day. The day 28 August comes from Prosper's Chronicle, as Schaff reports it; I did not open Prosper's Chronicle itself. Britannica says 'aged 75'. Possidius says 'he lived seventy-six years', counting the year he was in. Hippo fell soon after his death (Possidius 28: 'after Augustine's death the city of Hippo, abandoned by its inhabitants, was burned by the enemy').

buried.text: At Hippo, in front of Possidius and the others, after a service for him. The 1916 Roman Martyrology says his body was later taken to Sardinia, and then to Pavia in Italy by Liutprand, king of the Lombards. It is kept today in the church of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro there.
buried.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 31: 'in our presence, after a service was offered to God for the peaceful repose of his body, he was buried'; Roman Martyrology (1916), 28 August: 'His relics, owing to the invasion of barbarians, were first brought from his own city into Sardinia, and afterwards taken by Luitprand, king of the Lombards, to Pavia'; Roman Martyrology (1916), last day of February: 'At Pavia, the translation, from the island of Sardinia, of the body of St. Augustine, bishop, by Luitprand, king of the Lombards'; OCA, 'Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo': 'The Saint's Holy Relics are located in the Roman Catholic church of Saint Peter Ciel D' Oro Pavia, Italy'
buried.note: Possidius does not name the church or place of burial beyond Hippo. No source I read gives the year of the move to Pavia, so none is printed. Britannica is careful: 'The story was told that his mortal remains went to Sardinia and thence to Pavia ... Whatever the truth of the story'. Print it as the Martyrology tells it, with Britannica's caution.

also_called.source: Britannica, quick facts: 'Original Latin name: Aurelius Augustinus'

also_called.text: Blessed Augustine, in the Russian Church and the OCA.
also_called.source: OCA, 'Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo', commemorated on June 15; azbyka.ru: 'Блаженный Августин Аврелий, Иппонийский, епископ'; OCA Q&A: the Moscow Patriarchate's calendar lists him as 'the Blessed Augustine'
also_called.note: In Orthodox use 'Blessed' is a title, not the Catholic step before sainthood. The OCA's answer says so, and gives Blessed Xenia of St Petersburg as a saint with the same title.

also_called.text: Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, in Greek (Άγιος Αυγουστίνος Επίσκοπος Ιππώνος).
also_called.source: saint.gr, Orthodox Synaxaristis; Church of Cyprus, 'Μνήμη του Αγίου Αυγουστίνου, επισκόπου Ιππώνος (15 Ιουνίου)'

also_called.text: The Doctor of Grace, for his writing on grace against Pelagius.
also_called.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), quoting Specht: 'he deserves to be named the Doctor of the Church as well as the Doctor of Grace'
also_called.note: A traditional name, not a formal title of any church. Say 'often called'.

status.text: A saint and a Doctor of the Church to Catholics. On the Orthodox calendar as Blessed Augustine (Saint in Greek calendars). Kept by the Church of England and the Episcopal Church, and remembered by Lutherans.
status.source: USCCB Liturgical Calendar 2026 (28 August: 'Saint Augustine, Bishop and Doctor of the Church, Memorial'); Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Doctors of the Church'; OCA; saint.gr; Church of England Common Worship calendar; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; LCMS; Evangelical Lutheran Worship

patron_of.text: Britannica: brewers, printers, converts to Christianity and theologians, and the Augustinian orders.
patron_of.source: Britannica, 'What is St. Augustine the patron saint of?': 'the patron saint of brewers, printers, converts to Christianity, and theologians. He is also the patron of the Augustinians'
patron_of.note: Only Britannica checked. No church document naming these patronages was found.

in_art.text: As a bishop with a book and a pen. Often holding a heart, burning or pierced by an arrow. Sometimes beside a child with a shell at the seashore, from a medieval legend.
in_art.source: Schaff, 'Estimate of St. Augustin' (NPNF1-01): 'the man with upturned eye, with pen in the left hand, and a burning heart in the right (as he is usually represented)'; Shari Boodts, Medievalists.net, 'The child by the seaside' (2019): 'For Augustine, it was most often a book ... another object often associated with him is a heart, sometimes on fire or pierced by an arrow'
in_art.note: Boodts ties the pierced heart to Confessions IX.2.3 ('You have pierced our heart with your love'). The band painting (Champaigne) shows the burning heart, the pen and the books of Pelagius and Julian under his foot.

wrote.text: So much that, says Possidius, scarcely any student could read it all. Near the end of his life he reviewed 93 of his works, in 232 books, one by one. That count leaves out his letters and sermons.
wrote.source: Retractations, epilogue to Book 2 (Latin, augustinus.it): 'Haec opera nonaginta tria in libris ducentis triginta duobus me dictasse recolui'; Schaff, Prolegomena, note 26: 'In his Retractations, he himself reviews ninety-three of his works (embracing two hundred and thirty-two books, see ii. 67)'; Possidius, Life, chapter 18: 'so many things were dictated and published by him ... that scarcely any student would be able to read and know them all'
wrote.note: The OCA and azbyka.ru say Possidius counted about 1,030 writings; I did not see Possidius's list (the Indiculus) itself, so that number is in could_not_verify. The augustinus.it page blocked curl (HTTP 999); the Latin sentence was read through WebFetch.

pronounced.text: AW-guh-steen of HIP-oh. Also said aw-GUS-tin.
pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster gives AW-guh-steen first. The second form, aw-GUS-tin (or uh-GUS-tin), is also listed. Collins returned 403.

roles.text: Teacher of rhetoric: first grammar at Thagaste, then rhetoric at Carthage, Rome and Milan.
roles.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 1: 'he first taught grammar in his own town and then rhetoric at Carthage ... Subsequently [he taught] across the sea in the city of Rome and at Milan'
roles.note: Short line: 'At Carthage, Rome and Milan'.

roles.text: Monk: after his baptism he lived in common with friends at Thagaste for almost three years. As a priest he set up a monastery at Hippo where no one owned anything.
roles.source: Possidius, Life, chapters 3 and 5 ('almost three years'; 'no one should possess anything of his own')

roles.text: Priest: seized by the congregation at Hippo in 391 and ordained, weeping.
roles.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 4; Catholic Encyclopedia (1907): 'In spite of his tears Augustine was obliged to yield ... and was ordained in 391'
roles.note: Short line: 'Seized at Hippo, 391'. The Benedictine table in Schaff gives 389; modern references give 391.

roles.text: Bishop of Hippo: made co-bishop with the old bishop Valerius in 395 or 396, then bishop until his death in 430.
roles.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 8; Catholic Encyclopedia (1907): 'As bishop of Hippo (396-430)'; Merriam-Webster: 'bishop of Hippo (396-430)'; OCA: 'in 395, appointed him vicar bishop'
roles.note: Short line: 'Of Hippo, 396 to 430'. Sources split between 395 and 396 for the start.

catholic.text: 28 August, a memorial in the General Roman Calendar: 'Saint Augustine, Bishop and Doctor of the Church'. The 1916 Roman Martyrology also keeps 5 May for his conversion and 28 February for the moving of his body to Pavia.
catholic.source: USCCB, Liturgical Calendar for the Dioceses of the United States of America 2026, 28 August; Catholic Culture, 28 August 2026: 'Memorial of St. Augustine, Bishop and Doctor of the Church'; Roman Martyrology (1916), 28 August, 5 May and the last day of February
catholic.note: 1916 Martyrology, 28 August, exact: 'At Hippo Regius, in Africa, the birthday of St. Augustine, bishop and famous doctor of the Church.' 5 May, exact: 'In the same city [Milan], the conversion of St. Augustine, bishop and doctor of the Church, whom the blessed bishop Ambrose instructed in the Catholic faith, and baptized on this day.' (He was baptised at Easter 387, which was not 5 May; that is the Martyrology's wording, so do not repeat 'baptized on this day' as fact.) The February entry falls on the last day of February. The USCCB readings pages (bible.usccb.org) returned 403; the USCCB calendar PDF loaded. I did not check the current (2004) Martyrology.

orthodox.text: 15 June. Greek churches and the Church of Cyprus keep 15 June and call him Saint. The OCA keeps 15 June and calls him Blessed. The Russian Church keeps 15 June on the old calendar, which is 28 June on the civil calendar.
orthodox.source: saint.gr: 'Εορτάζει στις 15 Ιουνίου εκάστου έτους'; Church of Cyprus: 'Μνήμη του Αγίου Αυγουστίνου, επισκόπου Ιππώνος (15 Ιουνίου)'; OCA: 'Commemorated on June 15'; azbyka.ru: 'День памяти 28 июня'; OCA Q&A: 'his feast day is celebrated on June 15 [New Calendar]/ June 28 [Old Calendar]'
orthodox.note: GOARCH returned 403 and was not checked. Unlike Martin, the Orthodox churches agree on one day, 15 June; only the calendar differs. The OCA Q&A adds that he is 'listed as the final saint for the day'.

anglican.text: 28 August. Church of England: 'Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Teacher of the Faith, 430', a Lesser Festival. Episcopal Church (Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022): 'Augustine of Hippo, Bishop and Theologian, 430'.
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (printed in plain roman type: a Lesser Festival); The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, pages 375-376 (page header 'August 28')
anglican.note: In the LFF 2022 month table the day numbers and names are misaligned by pdftotext (it prints '26 Augustine of Hippo'); the entry page itself is headed 'August 28' and says 'Augustine died on August 28, 430'. Both churches keep Monica the day before, 27 August (LFF keeps her on 4 May).

lutheran.text: 28 August. Missouri Synod: 'Augustine of Hippo, Pastor and Theologian'. ELCA (Evangelical Lutheran Worship): 'Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, 430'.
lutheran.source: LCMS, Commemorations; Evangelical Lutheran Worship, The Church Year, assembly version (January 2006 draft, archived)
lutheran.note: The ELCA line is from the January 2006 draft of Evangelical Lutheran Worship, not the printed book. Same caveat as for Martin.

why_dates_differ.text: The West keeps the day he died, 28 August. No source I read says why the Orthodox keep 15 June.
why_dates_differ.source: Schaff, note 2 (Prosper: died 28 August 430); OCA: 'The Orthodox Church commemorates Saint Augustine on June 15, while the West commemorates him on August 28.'
why_dates_differ.note: The 1916 Martyrology calls 28 August his 'birthday', which it defines as the day a saint enters heaven (Martin's research).

numbers.text: He was sixteen when he and his friends stole pears they did not want and threw them to the pigs.
numbers.quote: carried away great loads, not to eat ourselves, but to fling to the very swine
numbers.source: Confessions, Book II, chapter 4 ('that sixteenth year of the age of my flesh', chapter 2; 'in that sixteenth year of my age', chapter 6)
numbers.note: CHECKER 2026-09-25: Corrected to 15. Augustine says "sixteenth year of my age" (Confessions 2.2, 2.3, 2.6), which is age 15. Page prints n 15, "In his sixteenth year".

numbers.text: From nineteen to twenty-eight he followed the Manichees, a sect he later wrote against.
numbers.quote: During this space of nine years, then, from my nineteenth to my eight and twentieth year
numbers.source: Confessions, Book IV, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia: 'The illusion had lasted nine years.'
numbers.note: CCEL prints 'eight and twentieth' across a line break; the check normalises spaces. CHECKER 2026-09-25: "From my nineteenth to my eight and twentieth year" is years of life, not ages; the page now says "His 19th to 28th years" and "In his nineteenth year" for the Hortensius.

numbers.text: Years as a priest or bishop, says Possidius, who was his friend for almost forty years.
numbers.quote: for he lived seventy-six years, almost forty of which he spent as a priest or bishop
numbers.note: Also in chapter 31: Possidius lived with him 'for almost forty years' of friendship.

numbers.text: In 232 books. He reread them all near the end and corrected what he now thought wrong. Letters and sermons are extra.
numbers.source: Retractations, Book 2, epilogue; Schaff, Prolegomena, note 26; Possidius, Life, chapter 28 ('this he himself censured and corrected')

numbers.text: At Hippo, in under two years after the relics of St Stephen arrived. He had the stories written up and read in church.
numbers.quote: It is not yet two years since these relics were first brought to Hippo-regius, and though many of the miracles which have been wrought by it have not, as I have the most certain means of knowing, been recorded, those which have been published amount to almost seventy at the hour at which I write.
numbers.source: City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8

numbers.text: Men from his monastery at Hippo sent out as bishops to other churches.
numbers.quote: And there were about ten men, holy and venerable, continent and learned, whom the most blessed Augustine furnished in answer to our request to various churches
numbers.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 11; Schaff: 'out of which ten bishops and many lower clergy went forth'
numbers.note: Possidius says 'about ten men' furnished to churches; Schaff calls them bishops. Possidius himself was one (bishop of Calama).

numbers.text: The Vandals besieged Hippo for almost fourteen months. He died in the third month.
numbers.quote: For almost fourteen months they shut up and besieged the city
numbers.note: A spare, if a number is dropped.

traits.title: quick to weep, and not ashamed of it
traits.text: He wept when the people of Hippo seized him to be ordained. He wept for his mother, and wrote that no one should laugh at him for it. On his deathbed he read the penitential psalms on the wall and wept.
traits.quote_exact: let him not laugh at me, but rather, if he be a man of a noble charity, let him weep for my sins against Thee
traits.quote_display: let him not laugh at me, but rather, if he be a man of a noble charity, let him weep for my sins against Thee
traits.source: Possidius, Life, chapters 4 ('he wept freely') and 31 ('he wept freely and constantly'); Confessions, Book IX, chapter 12

traits.title: could not live without friends
traits.text: He loved talk, jokes and reading with friends. After baptism he always lived in community, first with friends, then with his clergy.
traits.quote_exact: to discourse and jest with them; to indulge in an interchange of kindnesses; to read together pleasant books; together to trifle, and together to be earnest; to differ at times without ill-humour
traits.quote_display: to discourse and jest with them; to indulge in an interchange of kindnesses; to read together pleasant books; together to trifle, and together to be earnest; to differ at times without ill-humour
traits.source: Confessions, Book IV, chapter 8; Possidius, Life, chapters 3, 5 and 25
traits.note: This matches the Christian Personality Test's reading of the young Augustine (the Spark).

traits.title: no gossip at his table
traits.text: He had a couplet carved on his dining table against running down anyone who was not there. When bishop friends ignored it, he told them the verses would come off the table or he would leave the meal. Possidius was at the table.
traits.quote_exact: Who injures the name of an absent friend May not at this table as guest attend.
traits.quote_display: Who injures the name of an absent friend / May not at this table as guest attend.
traits.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 22 ('Both I and the others who were at the table experienced this.')
traits.note: Latin in Schaff: 'Quisquis amat dictis absentum rodere vitam, / Hanc mensam vetitam noverit esse sibi.'

traits.title: changed his mind in public
traits.text: He first held that no one should be forced into the Church. He later said he had been overcome by what he saw. In old age he reread all his books and corrected them in writing.
traits.quote_exact: For originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ, that we must act only by words, fight only by arguments, and prevail by force of reason
traits.quote_display: For originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ, that we must act only by words, fight only by arguments, and prevail by force of reason
traits.source: Letter 93, to Vincentius, section 17 (AD 408); Possidius, Life, chapter 28 (the Retractations)
traits.note: This is also a hard topic: see hard_topics.

traits.title: easily distracted, and honest about it
traits.text: He admits a dog chasing a hare, or a lizard catching flies, could pull his mind away from God.
traits.quote_exact: How is it, when sitting at home, a lizard catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into her nets, oftentimes arrests me?
traits.quote_display: How is it, when sitting at home, a lizard catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into her nets, oftentimes arrests me?

others_on_him.q: You are renowned throughout the whole world; Catholics revere and look up to you as the restorer of the ancient faith, and--which is a token of yet more illustrious glory--all heretics abhor you.
others_on_him.who: Jerome, writing to him in 418, after years of sharp letters
others_on_him.note: The CCEL text has double hyphens for dashes. New Advent URL opened: 'Letter 195 (Augustine) or 141 (Jerome)'.

others_on_him.q: you are challenging an old man, disturbing the peace of one who asks only to be allowed to be silent, and you seem to desire to display your learning.
others_on_him.who: Jerome, stung by the younger man's criticism, about 402
others_on_him.source: Augustine, Letters, Letter 72 (from Jerome), chapter 3, section 5
others_on_him.note: Pair it with Letter 195 to show the friendship grew.

others_on_him.q: But I believe that they were able to derive greater good from him who heard and saw him as he spoke in person in the church, and especially those who knew well his manner of life among men.
others_on_him.who: Possidius, his friend for almost forty years

others_on_him.q: I am struck with wonder at your wisdom, both in the books you have published and in this letter which you have not found it too great a burden to send me by way of intercession for those in distress.
others_on_him.who: Macedonius, a Roman governor in Africa, answering his plea for a prisoner

life_moments.title: The pears
life_moments.text: One night he and a gang of friends stripped a neighbour's pear tree. The pears were not even good, and he had better at home. They ate a few and threw the rest to the pigs. Nearly thirty years later he spent pages of his Confessions asking why. His answer: the pleasure was the theft itself.
life_moments.quote: having only eaten some of them; and to do this pleased us all the more because it was not permitted
life_moments.note: Year: the site's VERIFY.md dates the theft to 370; the Benedictine table in Schaff puts his return home at 370. He wrote the Confessions about 397 (Schaff's table). CHECKER 2026-09-25: when corrected to "Aged 15, about 370" (sixteenth year of his age).

life_moments.title: Lying to his mother
life_moments.text: He wanted to teach in Rome. His mother Monica followed him to the harbour to stop him or go with him. He told her he was only seeing a friend off. That night he sailed while she prayed in a chapel by the shore.
life_moments.quote: And I lied to my mother--and such a mother!--and got away.
life_moments.source: Confessions, Book V, chapter 8; Catholic Encyclopedia: 'In 383 Augustine, at the age of twenty-nine'
life_moments.note: The chapel is in the same chapter: 'a place quite close to our ship, where there was an oratory in memory of the blessed Cyprian. That night I secretly left, but she was not backward in prayers and weeping'. Checked.

life_moments.title: Take up and read
life_moments.text: He had given up his mistress, but not his old life. Weeping in a garden, he heard a child's voice from a house nearby chanting, 'Take up and read.' He opened Paul's letters and read Romans 13:13-14. His doubt was gone.
life_moments.quote: Take up and read; take up and read.
life_moments.source: Confessions, Book VIII, chapter 12; Catholic Encyclopedia: 'in the garden at Milan (September, 386)'; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022: 'the late summer of 386'
life_moments.note: Augustine says 'the voice as of a boy or girl, I know not which'. Keep 'a child's voice'.

life_moments.title: Baptised by Ambrose
life_moments.text: Ambrose, bishop of Milan, baptised him at Easter. His friend Alypius was baptised with him. So was his son Adeodatus, barely fifteen, whom he said was cleverer than many learned men.
life_moments.quote: He was barely fifteen years, yet in wit excelled many grave and learned men.
life_moments.source: Confessions, Book IX, chapter 6; Possidius, Life, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia: 'baptized by Ambrose on Easter Day, or at least during Eastertide'
life_moments.note: Adeodatus died young: Schaff's table has 388 or 389 ('Adeodatus, full of promise, dies'). Confessions IX.6: 'Quickly didst Thou remove his life from the earth'.

life_moments.title: His mother's last words
life_moments.text: Waiting for a ship home, Augustine and Monica stood at a window and talked about God. Days later she fell ill with a fever. She told her sons not to worry where she was buried. She died there, aged fifty-six.
life_moments.quote: Lay this body anywhere, let not the care for it trouble you at all. This only I ask, that you will remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.
life_moments.source: Confessions, Book IX, chapters 10 and 11 (fifty-six: 'the fifty-sixth year of her age, and the thirty-third of mine', chapter 11)
life_moments.note: Augustine gives his own age too: in his thirty-third year, so he was 32.

life_moments.title: Seized in church
life_moments.text: Visiting Hippo, he stood in the church as a layman. The bishop said the city needed a priest. The people laid hands on him and brought him forward, shouting, while he wept. Some thought he wept because he wanted to be a bishop. He told his friends he wept at the dangers of ruling a church.
life_moments.quote: they demanded it with great zeal and clamor, while he wept freely
life_moments.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 4; Augustine, Letter 21, to Valerius, sections 1 and 2
life_moments.note: Letter 21.2 confirms it in his own words: 'the tears which some of my brethren perceived me shedding in the city at the time of my ordination'.

summary.text: Yes, the early sources record them, of two kinds. Possidius tells of healings through Augustine's own prayers. Augustine himself tells of many healings he saw or checked, most at the shrines of martyrs.
summary.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 29; City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8
summary.note: Unlike Martin, there is no raising of the dead by Augustine. Keep the section shorter than Martin's. CHECKER 2026-09-25: Blind man at Milan: Confessions 9.7 says he asked his guide to lead him there and touched the bier with his handkerchief; "was brought to them" replaced. Possidius was Augustine's friend for almost forty years; he did not "live with" him all that time (bishop of Calama from his monastery). Page corrected in two places.

pledge.q: the things that I have seen in him and heard from him
pledge.note: Possidius writes of what he saw and heard himself. He was a member of Augustine's monastery and then a bishop nearby.

by_augustine.title: Demons driven out
by_augustine.text: Asked to pray for people possessed by demons, he prayed with many tears, and the demons left them.
by_augustine.quote: when asked to pray for certain demoniacs, he entreated God in prayer with many tears and the demons departed from the men
by_augustine.witness: Possidius says 'I know also' that it happened.

by_augustine.title: The sick man
by_augustine.text: While Augustine lay ill, a man brought a sick relative and asked him to lay his hand on him. Augustine said that if he had any such power he would have used it on himself first. The man said a dream had told him to come. So Augustine laid his hand on him, and the sick man went away healed.
by_augustine.quote: Go to the bishop Augustine that he may lay his hand upon him, and he shall be whole.
by_augustine.witness: Told by Possidius, who was in Hippo through the siege.
by_augustine.note: Augustine's own reply, exact: 'if he had any power in such things he would surely have applied it to himself first of all'.

seen_by_augustine.title: A blind man sees
seen_by_augustine.text: Ambrose found the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius. A blind man was brought to them and saw again. Augustine was in Milan at the time, and so was the emperor.
seen_by_augustine.quote: The miracle which was wrought at Milan when I was there, and by which a blind man was restored to sight, could come to the knowledge of many
seen_by_augustine.source: City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8; Confessions, Book IX, chapter 7
seen_by_augustine.note: Year: the finding of the relics was in 386 (Confessions IX.7 places it while Justina persecuted Ambrose). Check the year before printing.

seen_by_augustine.title: The surgeon's knife
seen_by_augustine.text: Innocentius, a former lawyer, had a fistula the surgeons had failed to heal. He dreaded a second operation and prayed with tears the night before. Augustine was there. Next morning the surgeon searched with his knife and found the place healed.
seen_by_augustine.quote: a cure wrought at Carthage, in my presence, and under my own eyes
seen_by_augustine.source: City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8
seen_by_augustine.note: When: Augustine says he and Alypius 'were not yet clergymen' and had come 'from abroad': that is on the way home from Italy, 388. The year is my inference; print 'Before he was a priest'.

seen_by_augustine.title: The trembling brother and sister
seen_by_augustine.text: Paulus and Palladia, from Caesarea in Cappadocia, had a shaking in all their limbs. They prayed at the relics of St Stephen in Hippo. On Easter morning Paulus fell as if asleep and rose healed. Three days later, while their story was read out in church, his sister was healed too.
seen_by_augustine.quote: The whole church was filled with the voices of those who were shouting and congratulating him.
seen_by_augustine.witness: Augustine was about to go into church. The young man came in and fell at his knees.
seen_by_augustine.source: City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8
seen_by_augustine.note: Year: 'about 425' is inferred from the relics arriving at Hippo about 424 and 'not yet two years'. Not in the text. Print 'At Easter'.

doubt.title: Doubted from the start
doubt.text: Augustine answers doubters in their own question: why do miracles not happen now? He also once doubted himself. In an early book he wrote that miracles had not been allowed to last into his own time. In his Retractations he corrected it, saying he had already known of the blind man at Milan.
doubt.quote: Why, they say, are those miracles, which you affirm were wrought formerly, wrought no longer?
doubt.source: City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8; On True Religion, chapter 25, section 47 (Latin); Retractations, Book I, chapter 13, section 7 (Latin)
doubt.note: On True Religion and the Retractations have no public-domain English that I found (Burleigh 1953 is in copyright), so quote only City of God here, or print the Latin with our own plain English marked as ours. Latin of On True Religion 25.47 (Latin Wikisource, per the quiz research, not re-fetched): 'nec miracula illa in nostra tempora durare permissa sunt'. Retractations Latin could not be fetched by curl (augustinus.it HTTP 999).

miracles.also_note: Augustine adds that such wonders stay local: 'these modern miracles are scarcely known even to the whole population in the midst of which they are wrought'.

feature.exact: for Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee.
feature.display: Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee.
feature.ctx: The first page of his Confessions, a book written as one long prayer to God. In Latin, 'fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te.'
feature.latin: fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te
feature.source: J. G. Pilkington (tr.), Confessions, NPNF 1st series vol. 1 (1886), CCEL plain text, marked Public Domain
feature.note: Pusey's older translation (Gutenberg 3296): 'Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.' Schaff's own rendering: 'Thou hast made us for Thyself, and our heart is restless till it rests in Thee.' New Advent: 'for You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.' All say the same; print Pilkington.

lines.exact: Too late did I love Thee, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love Thee! For behold, Thou wert within, and I without, and there did I seek Thee
lines.display: Too late did I love Thee, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love Thee! For behold, Thou wert within, and I without, and there did I seek Thee
lines.ctx: Looking back on the years he spent looking for God everywhere but within.
lines.note: Often quoted as 'Late have I loved you, beauty so old and so new'. Same passage, a newer translation.

lines.exact: Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet.
lines.display: Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet.
lines.ctx: His prayer as a young man, which he tells against himself: 'For I was afraid lest Thou shouldest hear me soon'.
lines.note: Really his. Latin: 'da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo' (not fetched).

lines.exact: Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt.
lines.display: Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt.
lines.ctx: A prayer he repeats in the Confessions. Pelagius could not bear it when he heard it quoted in Rome.
lines.note: Pelagius's reaction: On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53 ('could not bear; and contradicting somewhat too excitedly, nearly came to a quarrel').

lines.exact: Once for all, then, a short precept is given thee: Love, and do what thou wilt
lines.display: Once for all, then, a short precept is given thee: Love, and do what thou wilt
lines.ctx: Preaching on 1 John. He means that love must be the root of everything, even of correcting someone firmly.
lines.work: Homilies on the First Epistle of John
lines.note: Tr. H. Browne, NPNF1-07. Read the context: it goes on 'whether thou correct, through love correct'. It is not a licence to do anything.

lines.exact: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
lines.display: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
lines.ctx: The key to his City of God, written after Rome was sacked in 410.

lines.exact: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?
lines.display: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?
lines.ctx: He follows it with a pirate who told Alexander the Great that the only difference between them was the size of their fleets.
lines.note: The pirate story is in the same chapter (checked: 'that was an apt and true reply which was given to Alexander the Great by a pirate').

lines.exact: For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that thou mayest understand
lines.display: For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that thou mayest understand
lines.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John

lines.exact: I became a great puzzle to myself
lines.display: I became a great puzzle to myself
lines.ctx: After his closest friend died when they were both young.
lines.note: Also the famous Latin 'mihi magna quaestio factus sum' (not fetched).

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his. Quote Investigator found it first in Richard Lassels's travel book of 1670. Lassels only credited Augustine with the idea that the world is a great book. Augustine did write of 'a great book: the very appearance of created things', meaning that creation shows God.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Quote Investigator, 'The World Is a Book, and Those Who Do Not Travel Read Only One Page' (25 September 2025); Augustine, Sermon 68 (Mai 126), section 6, Latin: 'Est quidam magnus liber ipsa species creaturae'
misquoted_or_legend.note: QI: 'QI and other researchers have located no substantive evidence supporting the attribution to St. Augustine of Hippo.' Lassels 1670: 'if this world be a great book, as S. Augustine calls it ... They that never stir from home, read only one page of this Book'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his. The Augustine scholar James O'Donnell cannot find it in Augustine. It comes from the 1600s: Rupertus Meldenius, a Lutheran writing for peace in the Thirty Years' War, and before him Marco Antonio de Dominis in 1617.
misquoted_or_legend.source: James J. O'Donnell, 'A common quotation from "Augustine"?' (Georgetown)
misquoted_or_legend.note: O'Donnell: 'I cannot find the text in Augustine's own texts, nor does it sound Augustinian to me'. The 1617 de Dominis find is reported on the same page (from H. J. M. Nellen).

misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not in his works. The nearest is his Exposition of Psalm 72 (73): one who sings praise does not only praise, but praises gladly, and loves the one he sings to.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Fr John Zuhlsdorf, 'Who sings well prays twice... NOT!' (2006), quoting Enarratio in Psalmum 72, 1: 'Qui enim cantat laudem, non solum laudat, sed etiam hilariter laudat'
misquoted_or_legend.note: Zuhlsdorf: 'it does not say qui canit bis orat'. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1156) cites that passage for the saying. The public-domain English of Psalm 73 (Library of Fathers) was not checked.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his. It is usually credited to Ignatius of Loyola, and it is not his either. Its earliest form is in a Jesuit collection written about 150 years after Ignatius died.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Answers Magazine, 'St. Ignatius Said What?': 'the earliest appearance of this saying is to be found in a collection of Ignatian wisdom that was written 150 years after his death (see the Scintillae Ignatianae)'
misquoted_or_legend.note: The article says it is 'attributed to Ignatius (and sometimes to St. Augustine)'. The Scintillae Ignatianae is by Gabriel Hevenesi (1705); that year is not in the article, so leave it out. CHECKER 2026-09-25: WRONG in the draft: Horn says the popular form is first printed in 1868 (American Phrenological Journal); the Scintillae Ignatianae, 150 years after Ignatius, hold the REVERSED saying (pray as if all depended on you). Page corrected.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'Hope has two beautiful daughters. Their names are Anger and Courage.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: No one has found it in his works. An Augustine scholar told the writer Francis X. Maier the line is apocryphal.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Francis X. Maier, 'Hope and Her Daughters', First Things, 1 March 2021: 'A friend of mine who is an Augustine scholar tells me they're apocryphal, and I have never been able to find their source.'
misquoted_or_legend.note: Weaker source than the others; keep it as 'no one has found it'. CHECKER 2026-09-25: Maier says only that he never found its source and a friend who is an Augustine scholar calls it apocryphal; "No one has found it" overstated this. Page corrected.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He met a child on the beach trying to empty the sea into a hole, and learned he could never grasp the Trinity.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A medieval legend. It is not in his writings or in Possidius. It spread through the Golden Legend and later art.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Shari Boodts, 'The child by the seaside: a medieval story about Saint Augustine', Medievalists.net (2019)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Boodts calls it 'This late medieval legend' and says a written account is in the Golden Legend (13th century, Jacobus de Voragine; Caxton's English, 1483). Possidius, who knew him for forty years, does not tell it (checked: no seaside story in the Life). CHECKER 2026-09-25: WRONG in the draft: Boodts says the story is NOT in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend; Caxton added it to his English translation (1483) from an altar at Black Friars, Antwerp, and says he found it not in the legend in English, French or Latin. Page corrected.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He and Ambrose made up the Te Deum on the night of his baptism, singing verse by verse.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A later tradition, traced only to the end of the 700s. The Catholic Encyclopedia says scholars now generally reject it.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), 'Te Deum': 'The tradition that it was spontaneously composed and sung alternately by these saints on the night of St. Augustine's baptism (A.D. 387) can be traced back to the end of the eighth century ... This tradition is now generally rejected by scholars.'

misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his words. The nearest is in a letter giving a rule to nuns: correct faults 'with due love for the persons and hatred of the sin'.
misquoted_or_legend.note: with due love for the persons and hatred of the sin (exact, CCEL). The Latin 'cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum' is from the research file, not re-fetched.

friends_family_rivals.text: A Christian who wept and prayed for him for years. A bishop told her 'the son of these tears' could not be lost. She died at Ostia in 387, after his baptism.
friends_family_rivals.quote: it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish
friends_family_rivals.source: Confessions, Book III, chapter 12; Book IX, chapters 10 to 13
friends_family_rivals.note: Personality test: St Monica is the Deep Well in the Deep Well and Spark opposite pair.

friends_family_rivals.text: A pagan town councillor of Thagaste, won to faith by Monica near the end of his life.
friends_family_rivals.source: Confessions, Book II, chapter 3; Book IX, chapter 9

friends_family_rivals.text: Born to the woman he lived with for years and never named. Baptised with his father at fifteen, he died young.
friends_family_rivals.source: Confessions, Book IV, chapter 2; Book VI, chapter 15; Book IX, chapter 6
friends_family_rivals.note: The 'woman he never named' is correct: the Confessions give no name. The length ('about fifteen years') is NOT stated in the Confessions; leave it out.

friends_family_rivals.text: Sent away when Monica arranged a better marriage for him. She went back to Africa and vowed never to know another man. He wrote that his heart was 'racked, and wounded, and bleeding'.
friends_family_rivals.quote: my heart, which clave to her, was racked, and wounded, and bleeding
friends_family_rivals.note: A hard topic in its own right: he then took another mistress while waiting to marry (same chapter). State it plainly.

friends_family_rivals.text: Bishop of Milan. Augustine went to hear him preach for his style and stayed for what he said. He was struck that Ambrose read silently. Ambrose baptised him at Easter 387.
friends_family_rivals.quote: his eyes glanced over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were silent
friends_family_rivals.source: Confessions, Book V, chapters 13 and 14; Book VI, chapter 3; Possidius, Life, chapter 1
friends_family_rivals.note: Site pair line: 'Ambrose baptised Augustine in Milan, at Easter in 387.' Verified.

friends_family_rivals.text: From Thagaste. With him in the garden at Milan, baptised with him, and later bishop of Thagaste.
friends_family_rivals.source: Confessions, Book VIII, chapter 12; Book IX, chapter 6; Roman Martyrology (1916), 15 August: 'At Tagasta, in Africa, St. Alipius, bishop, who was the disciple of blessed Augustine, and the companion of his conversion'

friends_family_rivals.text: A member of his monastery who became bishop of Calama. He was in Hippo through the siege and wrote the first Life.
friends_family_rivals.source: Possidius, Life, preface and chapters 12, 28 and 31
friends_family_rivals.note: Bishop of Calama: NPNF1-01 footnotes: 'Possidius, a disciple of Augustin ... was the Bishop of Calama' and 'Crispinus was charged with an attempt to kill Possidius the bishop of Calama'. So the bishop ambushed and wounded by Donatists in Life chapter 12 was Possidius himself, though he tells it without naming himself.

friends_family_rivals.rel: sparring partner, then friend by letter
friends_family_rivals.text: They wrote to each other for more than twenty years. Augustine challenged his reading of Galatians and his new translation. Jerome told him not to trouble an old man. By 418 Jerome was praising him as 'the restorer of the ancient faith'.
friends_family_rivals.note: Site pair line verified: 'Jerome and Augustine wrote to each other for more than twenty years. Their early letters were sharp.' Letter 28 is about 394/395; Letter 195 is 418.

friends_family_rivals.text: A monk who taught that people can choose good by their own will. He could not bear Augustine's prayer 'Give what Thou commandest'. Augustine wrote against his teaching for about ten years.
friends_family_rivals.source: On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53; Possidius, Life, chapter 18 ('against these he labored for almost ten years')
friends_family_rivals.note: 'Taught that people can choose good by their own will' is our summary; the checker should compare it with the Catholic Encyclopedia's 'Pelagius and Pelagianism'.

friends_family_rivals.text: A rival African church that said only a pure clergy gave true sacraments. Their armed bands, the Circumcellions, once laid an ambush for him on the road.

friends_family_rivals.rel: an earlier teacher he argued against
friends_family_rivals.text: Augustine rejected Origen's hope that even the devil would one day be freed from punishment.
friends_family_rivals.quote: Origen was even more indulgent; for he believed that even the devil himself and his angels
friends_family_rivals.source: City of God, Book XXI, chapter 17
friends_family_rivals.note: Site pair line verified: 'Augustine argued against Origen's hope that everyone would be restored in the end.'

friends_family_rivals.text: After Augustine died, his defender Prosper of Aquitaine wrote a book against Cassian's teaching on grace and effort.
friends_family_rivals.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Semipelagianism': 'About 433 (434) he even ventured to attack Cassian himself ... in his book, "De gratia et libero arbitrio contra Collatorem"'
friends_family_rivals.note: Site pair line verified: 'Augustine's followers attacked Cassian's teaching on grace and effort.' Augustine himself never named Cassian.

how_he_died.big: He died of a fever on 28 August 430, in the third month of the Vandal siege of Hippo. He was about seventy-five.
paras: The Vandals had crossed from Spain and laid Africa waste. Possidius and other bishops took refuge in Hippo with him.
At table he told them what he was asking God: to free the city, or to make His servants brave, or to take him out of this world.

He had the shortest penitential psalms copied and hung on the wall by his bed. He read them and wept. For his last ten days he asked to be left alone to pray, except when the doctors came or food was brought.
He preached until his last illness. He made no will, because he owned nothing. He asked that the church's library be kept safe for the future.

prayer.exact: I would have you know that in this time of our misfortune I ask this of God: either that He may be pleased to free this city which is surrounded by the foe, or if something else seems good in His sight, that He make His servants brave for enduring His will, or at least that He may take me from this world unto Himself.

details: he commanded that the shortest penitential Psalms of David should be copied for him
he would look at these sheets as they hung upon the wall and read them; and he wept freely and constantly
He made no will, because as a poor man of God he had nothing from which to make it.
He repeatedly ordered that the library of the church and all the books should be carefully preserved for future generations.
Up to the very moment of his last illness he preached the Word of God in the church incessantly
how_he_died.last_words: None recorded. Possidius gives his prayer during the siege, not last words.

later.title: After his death
later.text: Hippo was abandoned and burned by the Vandals after he died. The 1916 Roman Martyrology says his body was later taken to Sardinia and then to Pavia. Britannica calls this a story that was told.
later.quote: after Augustine's death the city of Hippo, abandoned by its inhabitants, was burned by the enemy
later.source: Possidius, Life, chapter 28; Roman Martyrology (1916), 28 August; Britannica

how_he_died.note: Schaff quotes a deathbed passage from the 'Meditations' as his; the Meditations are medieval and not his (Schaff himself says 'I freely combine several passages', and the Catholic Encyclopedia lists them among spurious works: NOT checked). Do not use it.

is_he_a_saint.big: Yes to Catholics, Anglicans and Lutherans. The Orthodox keep him on their calendar as Blessed Augustine, and Greek calendars call him Saint.

churches.note: A Doctor of the Church. Memorial on 28 August.
churches.source: USCCB 2026 calendar; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Doctors of the Church': Gregory, Ambrose, Augustine and Jerome, whose feasts Boniface VIII ordered kept in 1298

churches.note: On the calendar on 15 June. 'Saint' in Greek calendars.
churches.source: OCA; azbyka.ru; saint.gr; Church of Cyprus

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England, 28 August

orthodox_caveat.text: Some Orthodox say he was never counted a saint, because of his teaching on predestination. The OCA answered that he is on the calendar and in the list of saints' names, that 'Blessed' is an Orthodox title and not a lower rank, and that there is no record of a formal glorification. The same answer sets out his teaching that everyone is born guilty of Adam's sin and that God chooses whom He saves before birth.
orthodox_caveat.quote_question: Blessed Augustine is respected in the Orthodox Church as a teacher, because of his wonderful defense of the Church's teachings against the various heresies of his time, but because of his errors in his teachings about predestination in the salvation of man, he was never considered a saint.
orthodox_caveat.quote_answer: in terms of a formal "canonization" or "glorification" of Augustine by the Orthodox Church there is of course no record
orthodox_caveat.quote_teaching: Everyone is born guilty of the original sin.
orthodox_caveat.source: OCA, Questions and Answers, 'St. Augustine & Original Sin' (quoting Prokurat and Golitzin, Historical Dictionary of the Orthodox Church, pp. 48-49)
orthodox_caveat.note: Straight quotes in the OCA page are HTML entities; the check normalises them. The filioque is often named too by Orthodox critics, but no source for that was fetched; leave it out or source it.

quotes.q: At Hippo Regius, in Africa, the birthday of St. Augustine, bishop and famous doctor of the Church.
quotes.who: The Roman Martyrology, 1916 edition, for 28 August
quotes.note: Reconstructed from the archive.org OCR, which reads 'A T HSppo Kegius, in Africa, the birthday of St. [mark] Augustine, bishop and famous doctor of the Church.' The check tests the unbroken span from 'Augustine, bishop and famous doctor' onward (passed). 'Hippo Regius' for 'HSppo Kegius' is an OCR correction.

main.exact: God, from whom to be turned away, is to fall: to whom to be turned back, is to rise again: in whom to abide, is to stand firm. God, from whom to go forth, is to die: to whom to return, is to revive: in whom to have our dwelling, is to live.
main.display: God, from Whom to be turned away, is to fall: to Whom to be turned back, is to rise again: in Whom to abide, is to stand firm. God, from Whom to go forth, is to die: to Whom to return, is to revive: in Whom to have our dwelling, is to live.
main.source: C. C. Starbuck (tr.), NPNF 1st series vol. 7 (1888)
main.note: Written soon after his conversion, in 386 or 387. Evangelical Lutheran Worship prints a prayer built on it as 'A prayer of Augustine of Hippo' ('to turn away from you is to fall, to turn toward you is to rise'). New Advent URL opened (HTTP 200, 'Soliloquies, Book I'); the text was checked in the CCEL volume.

short.exact: O Lord the one God, God the Trinity, whatever I have said in these books that is of Thine, may they acknowledge who are Thine; if anything of my own, may it be pardoned both by Thee and by those who are Thine. Amen.
short.display: O Lord the one God, God the Trinity, whatever I have said in these books that is of Thine, may they acknowledge who are Thine; if anything of my own, may it be pardoned both by Thee and by those who are Thine. Amen.
short.source: A. W. Haddan (tr.), NPNF 1st series vol. 3 (1887)
short.note: The last words of On the Trinity. New Advent URL opened (HTTP 200, 'On the Trinity, Book XV').

second.title: Fresco of Augustine
second.collection: Rome, Lateran, Cappella Sancta Sanctorum (per the Commons file title)
second.licence: Public domain. Commons tag {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}}. A photo of a fresco (a flat wall painting).

second.note: No public-domain Eastern icon of Augustine was found. Every Commons 'Greek Icon of Saint Augustinus of Hippo' file is a 20th-century icon sourced only to 'Websites' (348 to 912 px); its PD tag cannot be trusted, so it was rejected. So the second picture is the oldest portrait instead, painted about 120 to 170 years after he died, before the East-West split. It is below 1200 px (777 x 1143); it is the largest copy on Commons. The inscription at the foot reads DIVERSI DIVERSA PATRES (the rest of the line is not visible). The Commons page names Rome, Lateran, Sancta Sanctorum; I did not find a museum or scholarly page to confirm the place or the identification as Augustine. Already on the site at 500 px (site/public/img/early-christians/augustine-of-hippo.jpg). hub_card.groups_note: Hint 'fathers teachers' is right: a Latin Father and Doctor of the Church (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Doctors of the Church'). Not 'monks' as a group, although he lived under a monastic rule (Possidius 5); add 'monks' only if the hub wants every founder of a monastery there.
hub_card.lived_note: Hint '400s' is defensible: bishop 396-430, and his great works (City of God 413-426) are 400s. But he was born in 354 and converted in 386, so '300s' is equally true. personality_test.text: The Christian Personality Test names 'St Augustine, as a young man' among the saints of The Spark, and in the Deep Well and Spark opposite pair with his mother St Monica. This is the site's reading, not a church's.
personality_test.spark_card_text: Before his conversion he loved talk, jokes, reading together and friendly arguments. In his Confessions he calls it 'a restless youthfulness'. He is honest there, too, about where his love of pleasure had led him.

hard_topics.text: He first held that no one should be forced into the Church. By 408 he backed imperial laws that pressed the Donatists back into it, because he saw towns return and be glad of it. He asked the courts not to put them to death. Critics then and since say he gave Christians a warrant to persecute.
quotes: For originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ
But this opinion of mine was overcome not by the words of those who controverted it, but by the conclusive instances to which they could point.
our desire is rather that justice be satisfied without the taking of their lives or the maiming of their bodies in any part
I know not whether a greater number have been improved or made worse when alarmed under threats of such punishment at the hands of men as is an object of fear
hard_topics.source: Letter 93, to Vincentius, section 17 (408); Letter 133, to Marcellinus, section 1; Letter 95, to Paulinus and Therasia, section 3; Possidius, Life, chapter 12 (he interceded so Crispinus would not be fined)
hard_topics.note: Letter 133 is about Donatist clergy and Circumcellions who had killed one priest and maimed another; he still begged the judge to spare their lives and bodies. The critics' line ('a warrant to persecute') has NO quoted source here; drop it or source it. His own doubt, Letter 95.3, is the honest counterweight. CHECKER 2026-09-25: Letter 95.3 speaks of punishment in church discipline generally, not only of Donatists; page now says "Of punishing wrongdoers in general". CRITIC ADDED 2026-09-25 (verified): Pierre Bayle, A Philosophical Commentary on Luke 14:23, Part III (the remarks on Augustine's letters), English translation London 1708, page 370: 'He had a great share of Knowledg, but he had more Zeal.' Same page: changing one's opinion 'purely upon seeing the Successes of the Imperial Laws' is 'one of the wretchedest ways of Reasoning' (paraphrased on the page, not quoted: the OCR there is broken). Page 369 heading: Bayle will show Augustine's reasons 'are nevertheless false'. Page 370 also: he believed Augustine 'spoke as he thought', 'a well-meaning Man, and carry'd away by an over-ardent Zeal'. Title page: the letters 'usually alledg'd for the compelling of Hereticks, and particularly to justify the late Persecution in France'; Part III end: 'two Letters of St. Austin, printed apart by the Archbishop of Paris's Orders, to justify his own Conduct'. Fetched: archive.org bim_eighteenth-century_a-philosophical-commenta_bayle-pierre_1708_2 (OCR djvu text, long s), saved as bayle-1708-philosophical-commentary-part3.txt. The unsourced 'warrant to persecute' line is not used.

hard_topics.text: He taught that babies who die unbaptised are not saved, though they suffer 'the mildest punishment of all'. Later Catholic teaching softened this, and today the Catholic Church speaks of hope for them.
quotes: the mildest punishment of all will fall upon those who have added no actual sin, to the original sin they brought with them
hard_topics.note: The 'today the Catholic Church speaks of hope' line needs a source (International Theological Commission, 'The Hope of Salvation for Infants Who Die Without Being Baptised', 2007); NOT fetched. FETCHED 2026-09-25 (verified), vatican.va rc_con_cfaith_doc_20070419_un-baptised-infants_en.html, saved as itc-2007-hope-of-salvation-infants.txt. Section 22: later medieval authors' teaching 'modified the strict opinion of St. Augustine'. Section 102: 'serious theological and liturgical grounds for hope that unbaptised infants who die will be saved and enjoy the Beatific Vision'; 'reasons for prayerful hope, rather than grounds for sure knowledge'. Preliminary note: Cardinal Levada approved it for publication after the Holy Father's approval, 19 January 2007. Section 26 also calls it 'Augustine's stern view'.

hard_topics.text: He held that punishment in hell never ends, as eternal life never ends. He called those who hoped otherwise 'tender-hearted Christians' and argued with them kindly, but firmly.
quotes: I must now, I see, enter the lists of amicable controversy with those tender-hearted Christians
hard_topics.source: City of God, Book XXI, chapters 17 and 23

hard_topics.text: The Orthodox critique, in the OCA's own words: 'Everyone is born guilty of the original sin', and God's choice of whom He saves is made before birth. Catholics and Protestants built on him here; many Orthodox writers reject it.
quotes: Everyone is born guilty of the original sin.
hard_topics.note: CHECKER 2026-09-25: The OCA text does not say "many Orthodox reject it"; only the reader's question calls predestination his error. Page now says "Some Orthodox count it among his errors, as a question put to the OCA shows".

hard_topics.text: He lived for years with a woman he never names, and they had a son. He sent her away to make a better marriage, then took another mistress while he waited. He tells it himself.
quotes: And she went back to Africa, making a vow unto Thee never to know another man, leaving with me my natural son by her.
hard_topics.note: CHECKER 2026-09-25: Confessions 6.13 says his mother took great pains to get him a wife; nothing says "a better marriage". 6.15: torn from him "as an impediment to my marriage". Page corrected.

hard_topics.text: He counted marriage good, but ranked a life of continence above it, and saw lust as a wound left by the Fall. Britannica's summary: his views on sexuality 'were humane in intent but have often been received as oppressive in effect'.
quotes: marriage and continence are two goods, whereof the second is better
his views on sexuality were humane in intent but have often been received as oppressive in effect
hard_topics.source: Of the Good of Marriage, section 8; Britannica, 'Saint Augustine'
hard_topics.note: 'lust as a wound left by the Fall' is our summary; not checked against a line. Soften or source it (City of God XIV is the place).

hard_topics.text: No woman lived or stayed in his house, not even his widowed sister, a nun. Women saw him only with clergy present. Possidius admired this; many readers today find it hard.
quotes: No woman ever lived or stayed in Augustine's house, not even his own sister

tidbits.text: He hated Greek as a boy, understood not a word, and was driven on with threats and punishments; as a bishop he said his Greek scarcely counted as knowledge
tidbits.evidence: Confessions, Book 1, chapter 14 (ccel-npnf101.txt lines 3628-3640; free copy https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf101.vi.I_1.XIV.html): 'But why, then, did I dislike Greek learning ... The difficulty, in truth, the difficulty of learning a foreign language mingled as it were with gall all the sweetness of those fabulous Grecian stories. For not a single word of it did I understand, and to make me do so, they vehemently urged me with cruel threatenings and punishments.' Answer to Petilian, Book 2, chapter 38, section 91 (sources/people/augustine-of-hippo/na-14092.txt line 277, fetched 2026-09-25 from https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/14092.htm): 'I too indeed have attained to a very slight knowledge of the Greek language, scarcely to be called knowledge at all'. Schaff, Prolegomena (ccel-npnf101.txt lines 1087-1091) quotes the Latin, 'Graecae linguae perparum assecutus sum, et prope nihil', and dates the work to 400. 'As a bishop': he was bishop from about 395 (the page's path), and Schaff dates the work to 400.

tidbits.text: He had never heard of Antony; the two officials at Trier
tidbits.evidence: Confessions, Book 8, chapter 6 (ccel-npnf101.txt lines 11265-11310): Pontitianus, who 'held high office in the emperor's court', spoke 'of Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name was in high repute among Thy servants, though up to that time not familiar to us'; 'on a certain afternoon, at Triers ... came upon a certain cottage inhabited by some of Thy servants ... where they found a book in which was written the life of Antony'; one resolved on 'giving up his worldly employments to serve Thee', and the other 'replied that he would cleave to him'. They were 'Agents for Public Affairs'. The garden follows at once in chapter 8.

tidbits.text: He knew what time is until asked
tidbits.evidence: Confessions, Book 11, chapter 14 (ccel-npnf101.txt lines 16150-16152): 'What, then, is time? If no one ask of me, I know; if I wish to explain to him who asks, I know not.'

Possidius, Life, chapter 22 (possidius-life-weiskotten-1919.txt line 205): 'His spoons only were silver, but the vessels in which food was served were earthen, wooden or marble; yet this was not from the compulsion of necessity, but from the choice of his own will.'

Confessions, Book 1, chapter 7 (ccel-npnf101.txt lines 3305-3310): 'I myself have seen and known an infant to be jealous though it could not speak. It became pale, and cast bitter looks on its foster-brother ... when the fountain of milk is flowing fresh and abundant, one who has need should not be allowed to share it'.
